messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 49
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

Vignette:
Julian, a 49-year-old fashion designer known for his sharp, architectural silhouettes, presented as a man meticulously in control, yet his hands trembled slightly as he spoke. The trauma occurred eight months prior, on what should have been a triumphant evening at a gallery opening celebrating a collaboration. He and his wife, Claire, were surrounded by the familiar hum of the city’s art scene when she collapsed. The memory of that moment, he explained, is not a continuous film but a series of searingly sharp, disconnected images. He can recall with perfect, agonizing clarity the exact slate-grey of the polished concrete floor and the way the light caught the sequins on her dress as she fell. He remembers the sound of her sharp, aborted gasp. But the minutes that followed are a complete blank, a chasm of lost time until the piercing wail of the ambulance siren filled the space. It is this blankness that haunts him most. In the quiet of the night, he is certain that he failed her in those missing moments, that his panic rendered him useless. When he tries to force the memory, a wave of guilt so profound washes over him that he feels physically ill, and he has to stop, his heart hammering against his ribs as if trying to escape.

In the weeks following Claire’s stroke and her slow, arduous recovery, Julian’s life became a fortress against silence and stillness. He began working with a ferocity that alarmed his colleagues, staying late in his studio, losing himself in the minutiae of stitching and draping. He needed to keep his mind occupied at all times; if his thoughts were a frantic storm of fabric weights and design sketches, there was no room for the intrusive image of the sequined dress against the grey floor. At home, the television was always on, a constant stream of noise to fill the space where his own thoughts might otherwise echo. The thought suppression was a conscious, exhausting effort. He would feel the memory begin to surface—the smell of champagne, the low thrum of the crowd—and would immediately force himself to mentally recite the day’s production schedule, a desperate incantation against the past.

This constant state of high alert has reshaped his world. He experiences strong physical reactions to the most mundane of cues. A siren screaming down a distant avenue can leave him breathless and sweating. The other day, an intern in his studio tripped over a bolt of fabric, and Julian felt a jolt of pure horror, his vision narrowing as he was thrown back into the gallery. He had to retreat to his office, overwhelmed by a shame he couldn't articulate. His sleep is fractured, offering little respite. He resists going to bed, knowing that in the dark, the memories return with a vengeance. He often wakes up abruptly, drenched in sweat, the feeling of absolute dread clinging to him like a shroud.

The future, once a landscape of shared dreams with Claire, has become a source of profound terror. Making any plans feels like tempting fate, an act of hubris he is no longer willing to risk. When Claire, now walking with a cane but steadily improving, recently brought up planning a trip to Kyoto for their anniversary next year, Julian felt a surge of panic. He couldn't commit to something so far away, something that required a belief in a stable, predictable future he no longer possessed. He deflected, saying they should focus on the present, a response that he saw land with a quiet thud of disappointment between them. This avoidance has become a pattern, a new, painful distance in their marriage. It was this growing chasm, and the realization that he was losing her all over again, that finally propelled him to seek help. He confessed in his first session that he feels fundamentally broken, and what frightens him most is the belief that the joy and safety he once took for granted are gone forever, lost in those few blank minutes on the gallery floor.
